# Security & Coordinated Disclosure (CVD) — Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Security*

# Found something? Tell us first.

We practice coordinated disclosure across all products. This page defines exactly what you can expect from us — response times, severity handling and legal safe harbor for researchers.

[Report a vulnerability](mailto:important@hartwell-labs.pl?subject=Security%20report%3A%20%5Bproduct%5D) → [security.txt](https://hartwell-labs.pl/.well-known/security.txt)

## How disclosure works

Send a report to the security contact below. Include a description, reproduction steps and affected product/version. We will:

48 hours
Acknowledgment.
You receive a confirmation with a tracking reference.
Days 2–7
Triage & severity.
We reproduce, classify per the table below and agree on a coordination timeline with you.
Fix
Remediation.
Patch developed, tested and released per the severity SLA. You get pre-release access to verify the fix.
Release
Public disclosure.
Advisory published with credit (opt-in). Nothing is published before a fix ships, unless the vulnerability is already being exploited.

### Severity & response targets

| Severity (CVSS 3.1) | Examples | Acknowledgment | Fix target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Severity (CVSS 3.1) | Examples | Acknowledgment | Fix target |
| Critical 9.0–10.0 | RCE, auth bypass, signature-verified pipeline escape | 48 hours | 7 days |
| High 7.0–8.9 | Privilege escalation, detection evasion by design | 48 hours | 30 days |
| Medium 4.0–6.9 | Info leaks, weak defaults in optional modes | 48 hours | 90 days |
| Low 0.1–3.9 | Hardening opportunities, documentation gaps | 48 hours | Best effort |

### Supported versions

| Product | Supported line | Latest release | Security fixes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Product | Supported line | Latest release | Security fixes |
| talus-process-monitor | v0.8.x | v0.8.2 (2026-09-23) | Yes |
| Externum | v4.3.x | v4.3.0 (2026-09-23) | Yes |
| All other products | latest | see releases page | Yes |
| Older releases | — | — | Unsupported |

### Safe harbor

We consider security research conducted in good faith and in accordance with this policy to be authorized. We will not pursue legal action against researchers who: use only their own accounts and test data, avoid service degradation, give us reasonable time to remediate before public disclosure, and do not access data belonging to other users. If you are unsure whether your activity fits, contact us first — we will help you draw the line.

### Hall of Fame

No external reports yet — the list is empty on purpose, not by omission. If you find a real issue in our products, this is where your name goes.

Impatient? Try to break our products — the challenge lives in the hack-the-lab repository.

#### Your name here

opt-in credit

We credit only with your explicit consent — anonymous acknowledgment ("a friendly researcher") works just as well.

# Talus Field Guide — deployment & tuning playbook | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

On this page

← talus-process-monitor

## Talus Field Guide

Deployment & tuning playbook for real Linux servers. Written by the author — every flag here is a real interface of the agent, nothing invented.

### 1. Pick your deployment mode before anything else

| Mode | Command | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Mode | Command | Use when |
| Observe | sudo process-monitor monitor | First week. Learn what normal looks like on YOUR hosts. Zero risk. |
| Pipeline | sudo process-monitor monitor --json | You already run a log stack (rsyslog, Loki, SIEM). Detection without response. |
| EDR | sudo process-monitor monitor --auto-kill | Hosts that hold things worth keeping, after tuning. Requires Enterprise license. |

Rule of thumb: never start in EDR mode. Tune in Observe, graduate to EDR. A wrong kill on a backup job is worse than a slow alert.

### 2. Install and sanity-check in five minutes

```
# Option A: pip installer (pulls the prebuilt release binary, no compiler needed) pip install talus-process-monitor talus-monitor install # downloads the agent from GitHub Releases # (v0.8.3: eBPF object is embedded — no .o install step) # Option B: cargo (builds from crates.io) cargo install process-monitor # Option C: build from source git clone https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/talus-process-monitor.git cd talus-process-monitor && ./build.sh # TUI variant, ~1.7MB # or: ./build.sh --web # + REST API, WebSocket, Prometheus (Enterprise) ./install.sh # user-local install (default) sudo ./install.sh --system # /usr/local system-wide # 5-second end-to-end self-diagnostic (eBPF loads? events flowing?): sudo process-monitor monitor --diagnose
```

If --diagnose completes cleanly, the pipeline works end-to-end on your kernel. If it fails: check you are root (or CAP_BPF/CAP_SYS_ADMIN, as in the Docker example), and that BTF is available (ls /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux).

### 3. Tuning the one knob that matters: the threshold

Talus alerts when a process opens N or more files within 1 second (default --alert-threshold 50). That single number is your false-positive dial:

    - Backups, sync jobs, media encoding — these legitimately touch hundreds of files per second. Run during a real backup window; if Talus flags the backup process, raise the threshold above the observed rate (e.g. --alert-threshold 400 ).
    - Typical web/API hosts — the default 50 rarely fires on legitimate traffic. Keep it.
    - Paranoid mode (tiny document sets, archives) — --alert-threshold 20 . Expect noise; tune or accept.

```
# Measure what normal looks like on this host: sudo process-monitor monitor --benchmark 30 # throughput + hot processes # Narrow the view to the file types you actually protect: sudo process-monitor monitor --filter-ext pdf sudo process-monitor monitor --filter-ext enc
```

FP triage method: run --json for 24h into a file, jq the alerts, and whitelist the two or three noisy legitimate processes by adjusting the threshold — not by disabling the agent. One evening of work, once per host type.

### 4. Ship it as a service

```
# /etc/systemd/system/talus.service [Unit] Description=Talus eBPF ransomware tripwire After=network.target [Service] ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/process-monitor monitor --json --alert-threshold 400 Restart=always RestartSec=5 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

```
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now talus journalctl -u talus -f # watch the NDJSON stream
```

### 5. MeMLP — the neural layer, when to switch it on

--memlp enables the online-training detection engine. It learns from live events and saves a checkpoint every 30 seconds:

```console
sudo process-monitor monitor --memlp --memlp-checkpoint /var/lib/talus/memlp.json
```

    - Switch it on after the threshold is sane — it learns from the stream you give it.
    - The checkpoint persists across restarts: the model you trained stays yours.

### 6. Enterprise wiring (license → dashboard → exports)

```
# Activate your license (no root required): process-monitor license activate KEY process-monitor license verify # Web dashboard + REST API + Prometheus (build with ./build.sh --web first): sudo process-monitor monitor --web 0.0.0.0:8080 --auto-kill # Stream detections into your data stack: sudo process-monitor monitor --auto-kill \ --kafka-brokers localhost:9092 --kafka-topic talus-detections \ --clickhouse http://localhost:8123 \ --memgraph http://localhost:7474
```

Kafka/ClickHouse/Memgraph flags are independent — wire only what your stack already has. Nothing leaves the host by default.

### 7. Runbook: an alert fired — now what

    - In Observe/Pipeline mode: identify the process from the JSON event (pid, comm, exe). If it is not a known job — stop it, snapshot the directory tree, check for rename chains and new .enc -style extensions.
    - In EDR mode: Talus already killed the process (SIGKILL at threshold breach). Verify with journalctl -u talus | grep kill , then preserve evidence before restoring from backup.
    - After any incident: re-run --diagnose , review whether the threshold should move, and keep the 24h JSON window as evidence.

### 8. Honest limits

    - Talus watches file-event behaviour . It is not an antivirus, not a network IDS, and it will not catch a threat that touches zero files.
    - eBPF requires BTF/CO-RE support (recent kernels; the Docker runbook mounts /sys/kernel/btf explicitly). Old LTS boxes need a plan.
    - One threshold for the whole host: workloads with wildly different IO profiles on one box need either separate hosts or a higher threshold.

### Frequently asked questions

Which Talus deployment mode should I start with?

Start in Observe mode (sudo process-monitor monitor) for about a week. It is detection-only with zero risk of a wrong kill, and it teaches you what normal file activity looks like on your hosts. Graduate to Pipeline mode (--json) when you run a log stack, and to EDR mode (--auto-kill) only after tuning, on hosts that hold things worth keeping.

How do I install Talus without a compiler?

pip install talus-process-monitor, then run talus-monitor install — the Python installer pulls the prebuilt release binary (~4 MB) from GitHub Releases, no Rust toolchain needed. Alternatively cargo install process-monitor builds from crates.io, or ./build.sh compiles from source.

What threshold should I set for Talus alerts?

Talus alerts when a process opens N or more files within 1 second (default --alert-threshold 50). Keep 50 on typical web/API hosts, raise it above the observed rate of legitimate write-heavy jobs like backups (e.g. --alert-threshold 400), or lower it to 20 in paranoid mode for tiny document sets. Run monitor --benchmark 30 to measure what normal looks like on your host first.

What Linux kernels does Talus support?

Talus needs eBPF with BTF/CO-RE support, which means recent kernels. Check with ls /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux — if that file exists, the agent loads. The Docker runbook mounts /sys/kernel/btf explicitly. Old LTS kernels without BTF need a separate plan; there is no kernel module fallback by design.

An alert fired — what do I do first?

Do not panic-kill. First identify the process from the alert output, then check whether it is a legitimate write-heavy job (backup, sync, media encoding) that simply crossed the threshold — if so, raise the threshold instead of disabling the agent. If the process is unknown, snapshot-preserve the target directories before any response, then pause or kill. The runbook section above walks through this decision step by step.

### Want the rest of the product?

Capabilities, the sixty-second start and the component licensing table are on the product page. The agent itself is free and MIT forever — the Enterprise license adds auto-kill, the web dashboard and the Kafka/ClickHouse exports.

## Page content

*Flagship · Rust · eBPF*

# Talus Process Monitor — behavioral ransomware detection that answers with a kill signal.

talus-process-monitor hooks syscall tracepoints in the Linux kernel, scores per-process open-rates in one-second windows and terminates the encryptor with SIGKILL — guardrailed, whitelist-aware, and never at the cost of the host. One static binary. No kernel modules. No telemetry.

[Try 14 days free](mailto:metaforicmail@proton.me?subject=Talus%2014-day%20trial&body=Please%20send%20me%20a%2014-day%20evaluation%20license%20for%20Talus.%0A%0AMachines:%201) → [Deployment guide](https://hartwell-labs.pl/docs#talus) → [Source ↗](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/talus-process-monitor)

$50 per machine per year · fleet tier from $30 · one key per machine, delivered by email on payment · VAT invoice · or request a quote by email

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **~280k** | events per second, single core |
| **7.6%** | sustained CPU under synthetic load |
| **<1s** | verdict to SIGKILL, same second |
| **188** | tests in the CI suite, every push |

## Three layers, one binary.

*What it does*

Detection is the easy half. Talus ships the half nobody writes up: the response path.

#### Detect: behavior, not signatures

Mass file-opens scored per process in 1s windows; canary reads, mass-delete and exfiltration-spike detectors. Signature-free — catches strains nobody has named yet.

#### Respond: SIGKILL in the same second

When the verdict fires, the offending process is killed immediately. Guardrails, per-path whitelists and canary verification keep it fast without being reckless.

#### Contain: Landlock & seccomp self-sandboxing

The agent sandboxes itself before it starts watching: no kernel modules, no writable footprint outside its own directory, verified by its own tests.

#### Ship: SIEM, Kafka, ClickHouse, MemGraph

Forward alerts as RFC5424 or CEF, stream raw events to Kafka, persist to ClickHouse, explore process lineage in MemGraph. Self-hosted, your infrastructure.

## From pip to live dashboard.

*Sixty-second start*

```console
pip install talus-process-monitor
```

```console
talus-monitor install
```

```console
sudo talus --web 10.0.0.5:8443
```

```console
talus-monitor selftest --canary
```

The canary self-test simulates a ransomware burst with harmless file operations and prints the real verdict — detection proof on your hardware in under a minute. Full flags and tuning: /docs and the Field Guide.

## Real-world guardrails, real-world results.

*Built for production*

Talus runs where attacks happen: inside the kernel, on your hosts, on your terms.

#### eBPF-native

Kernel-level process events via eBPF. No kernel modules, no reboot, near-zero overhead.

#### Privacy-first

Runs entirely on your servers. No cloud dependency, no telemetry, no third-party servers.

#### Instant activation

Buy through Stripe → activate in under 5 minutes. Ed25519-signed keys, server-side seats.

#### Active development

Ship every week. See the changelog and documentation.

## From install to kill-switch.

*Three minutes, three steps*

1

#### Install

pip install talus-process-monitor && talus license activate <KEY> — eBPF probes attach to the kernel in seconds, zero config.

2

#### Activate

One key per machine. Seats enforced server-side. 30-day Enterprise trial on first run — no card required.

3

#### Monitor

Real-time process events, anomaly alerts, SIGKILL under 1s. Fleet dashboard at your domain.

## Standalone Linux, not Kubernetes.

*Why Talus?*

Talus monitors individual servers and small fleets — no sidecars, no cluster, no Helm.

## Frequently asked.

*Questions*

How is Talus different from Falco or Tetragon?

Talus is built for standalone Linux servers, not Kubernetes. No sidecars, no cluster, no Helm charts — deploy one binary and monitor.

What are the system requirements?

Linux kernel 5.8+ with BTF enabled. Ubuntu 20.04+, Debian 11+, RHEL 8+, Arch. Root for eBPF attachment. Minimal RAM/CPU overhead.

How does licensing work?

Single: one server, $50 / 200 PLN per year. Fleet: per-node, minimum 10 nodes ($30 / 117 PLN per node/year). Annual subscription, instant activation, cancel anytime.

Can I try before buying?

Yes — a 30-day Enterprise trial starts automatically on first run, no credit card. Need longer? Ask for 14 more days.

Is my data sent to the cloud?

No. Talus runs entirely on your servers. The optional fleet dashboard aggregates from your own nodes — no third-party servers.

What payment methods do you accept?

Stripe checkout — card payments globally, priced in USD or PLN.

### 2. Typography and layout

- Body: **Inter** (400/500/600/700), 16px, `line-height: 1.65`, kolor `--txt`.
- Kod inline i bloki: **JetBrains Mono** (400/600).
- Oba kroje z Google Fonts, z `preconnect` do `fonts.googleapis.com` i `fonts.gstatic.com`.
- `.container`: `max-width: 1100px`, wycentrowany, padding 24px po bokach.
- Nagłówek: sticky, wysokość **64px**, tło `rgba(255,255,255,.88)` z `backdrop-filter: blur(10px)`, dolna linia 1px `--border`, `z-index: 50`.
- Stopka: tło `--bg-subtle`, górna linia `--border`, siatka wielokolumnowa + cienka linia legalna.
- Przyciski: wysokość 44px, `border-radius: 10px`, `font-weight: 600`; `.btn-primary` wypełniony akcentem, `.btn-secondary` z obramowaniem.
- Breakpointy w CSS: `@media (max-width: 720px)`, `@media (max-width: 820px)`, `@media (max-width: 420px)` — na wąskich ekranach nawigacja w nagłówku jest ukrywana.

## Frequent questions
How is Talus different from Falco or Tetragon?

Talus is built for standalone Linux servers, not Kubernetes. No sidecars, no cluster, no Helm charts.

What are the system requirements?

Linux 5.8+ with BTF. Ubuntu 20.04+, Debian 11+, RHEL 8+, Arch. Root for eBPF.

Can I change the number of nodes later?

Yes — fleet is a subscription; change seat count in your Stripe portal any time, prorated.

Do I get a refund if not satisfied?

14-day money-back guarantee on request — email contact@hartwell-labs.pl.

# Talus vs bpftrace — continuous monitoring vs one-off tracing

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

Comparison

## Talus vs bpftrace

bpftrace is the right tool for one-off tracing and debugging. Talus is for when you want those events always on — with alerts, auto-response, and a fleet view.

| Capability | Talus | bpftrace |
|---|---|---|
| Capability | Talus | bpftrace |
| eBPF kernel events | ✅ | ✅ |
| Continuous monitoring | ✅ daemon-less | ❌ run once |
| Anomaly detection | ✅ | ❌ |
| SIGKILL response | ✅ | ❌ |
| Fleet dashboard | ✅ | ❌ |
| Alerts (webhook/SIEM) | ✅ | ⚠️ manual export |
| Skill floor | admin | ⚠️ BPF scripting |
| Price / year | $50 | Free |

Which should I run on a host?

Use bpftrace to debug, use Talus to guard. They compose: Talus runs silently; bpftrace drops in when you need to look closer.

See pricing →

- Kod inline i bloki: **JetBrains Mono** (400/600).
- Oba kroje z Google Fonts, z `preconnect` do `fonts.googleapis.com` i `fonts.gstatic.com`.
- `.container`: `max-width: 1100px`, wycentrowany, padding 24px po bokach.
- Nagłówek: sticky, wysokość **64px**, tło `rgba(255,255,255,.88)` z `backdrop-filter: blur(10px)`, dolna linia 1px `--border`, `z-index: 50`.
- Stopka: tło `--bg-subtle`, górna linia `--border`, siatka wielokolumnowa + cienka linia legalna.
- Przyciski: wysokość 44px, `border-radius: 10px`, `font-weight: 600`; `.btn-primary` wypełniony akcentem, `.btn-secondary` z obramowaniem.
- Breakpointy w CSS: `@media (max-width: 720px)`, `@media (max-width: 820px)`, `@media (max-width: 420px)` — na wąskich ekranach nawigacja w nagłówku jest ukrywana.

# Talus vs Falco — standalone Linux eBPF monitoring

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

Comparison

## Talus vs Falco

Falco is the CNCF standard for runtime security — but it was built for Kubernetes. Talus is built for standalone Linux servers: one static binary, no sidecars, no cluster.

| Capability | Talus | Falco |
|---|---|---|
| Capability | Talus | Falco |
| eBPF kernel events | ✅ | ✅ |
| Standalone host (no K8s) | ✅ | ⚠️ needs k8s or heavy daemon |
| No sidecars / daemonset | ✅ | ❌ |
| Auto response (SIGKILL) | ✅ under 1s | ❌ alerts only |
| Process tree view | ✅ | ⚠️ limited |
| Fleet dashboard | ✅ | ⚠️ via integrations |
| Setup time | 5 min | 30+ min |
| Price / node / year | $50 | Free (but ops heavy) |

Who is this comparison for?

Teams monitoring individual Linux servers, small fleets, edge, or air-gapped hosts where a Kubernetes operator is not an option.

View Talus pricing →Try 14 days free →

← Back to product

# Talus vs Tetragon — standalone eBPF vs Cilium/K8s

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

Comparison

## Talus vs Tetragon

Tetragon is a Cilium/Hubble project that excels inside Kubernetes. Talus exists for the rest of your fleet — individual Linux servers, edge, and small clusters where the CNI stack is not on the menu.

| Capability | Talus | Tetragon |
|---|---|---|
| Capability | Talus | Tetragon |
| eBPF kernel events | ✅ | ✅ |
| Requires Kubernetes | ❌ | ⚠️ yes (Cilium) |
| CNI / sidecar dependency | ❌ none | ⚠️ Cilium+Hubble |
| Standalone host deploy | ✅ 1 binary | ❌ |
| Auto response | ✅ SIGKILL | ⚠️ via policy |
| Fleet dashboard | ✅ | ⚠️ via Hubble |
| Setup time | 5 min | 30+ min (k8s) |
| Price / node / year | $50 | Free (ops cost) |

When to pick Tetragon

Inside Kubernetes, with Cilium already deployed, Tetragon is the richer signal. On a bare server or non-K8s fleet, Talus is simpler.

Compare pricing →

# Hartwell AI — Service Terms — Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

Legal

## Hartwell AI

Version 1.0 · effective 19 November 2026 · master terms · privacy policy

A chat interface that sends your prompts to a language-model provider using your own API key (BYOK).

### 1. Scope

These terms apply to Hartwell AI and form part of our Terms of Service.

We do not provide a model and do not handle billing with the model provider. You use your own API key and pay the provider directly under its pricing.

### 2. Your key and your prompts

Your key is used only to forward requests to the provider you chose. Prefer a key with limited scope that you can revoke.

Prompts are sent to that provider to generate a response. We do not use prompts or outputs to train models. We cannot guarantee the provider does not retain them, so do not submit special-category data, other people’s personal data without a basis, trade secrets or professional secrets.

The provider’s terms and privacy policy apply to its processing.

### 3. Output

Output is a draft, not a fact. It can be incomplete, outdated or wrong. Verify before relying on it, especially in law, medicine, finance and security.

The service does not provide legal, medical, financial or other professional advice.

### 4. Acceptable use

Do not use the service to generate unlawful content, including sexual material involving minors, incitement to violence, weapons-of-mass-destruction instructions, malware, or content that infringes third-party rights. Do not bypass provider safeguards or hammer the service with automated bulk requests.

### 5. Availability and liability

The service depends on a third party and is provided as is, without a service level. We are not liable for provider outages, refusals, price changes or API changes, or for decisions you take based on generated output, to the extent permitted by law.

## Aurora

An operating system that runs entirely in the browser: kernel, window manager, filesystem and applications.

### 1. Relationship to the master terms

## fortis

Version 1.0 · effective 19 November 2026 · master terms · privacy policy

Chain-of-trust attestation for embedded systems built on RISC-V.

### 1. Relationship to the master terms

These product terms apply to fortis and form part of our Terms of Service. If they conflict with the master terms, these terms prevail for fortis.

The software is open source under the MIT License. Nothing in these terms restricts, replaces or conditions the rights the MIT License grants you; where the licence and these terms differ on the use of code, the licence prevails.

### 2. Licence

Permission is granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy of the software and associated documentation, to deal in it without restriction, including the rights to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell copies, subject to including the copyright notice and permission notice in all copies or substantial portions.

The software is provided “as is”, without warranty of any kind, express or implied, including merchantability, fitness for a particular purpose and non-infringement. In no event are the authors or copyright holders liable for any claim, damages or other liability arising from the software or its use.

Commercial add-ons, hosted features or paid packs, where offered, are governed by their own terms: None — MIT licensed in full.

### 3. Permitted use and restrictions

Use it with hardware you control. Do not represent attestation results as certification by Hartwell Labs.

You must not use the software to attack, scan or interfere with systems you do not own or have written authorisation to test, and must not remove copyright or attribution notices from redistributed copies.

You are responsible for complying with the law applicable to you, including export control and sanctions rules.

### 4. Support and updates

Support is provided through public repositories and documentation on a best-effort, community basis, with no guaranteed response time and no obligation to fix any defect.

You are responsible for testing updates before deploying them in production and for keeping backups.

### 5. Liability and risk

Attestation verifies what the software measures, not that the hardware is free of compromise. A valid chain does not guarantee a trustworthy device.

To the extent permitted by law, we are not liable for any damage arising from the use or inability to use the software. Nothing in these terms limits liability that cannot be limited by law, or the rights of consumers under mandatory provisions.

## Page content

Legal

## hack-the-lab

Version 1.0 · effective 19 November 2026 · master terms · privacy policy

Participation rules for our public security challenges.

### 1. Scope of authorisation

These terms apply to hack-the-lab and form part of our Terms of Service.

We authorise testing only against the targets, instances and endpoints we explicitly publish for a challenge, and only in the manner described. Everything else is out of scope.

You must not attack our websites, mail, infrastructure, staff or other participants, run denial-of-service tests, or access data belonging to other players.

### 2. Flags, write-ups and disclosure

Flags are confidential until a challenge is retired. Publishing flags, solutions or write-ups for an active challenge may result in disqualification.

Found vulnerabilities in our own infrastructure must be reported privately under /security; do not exploit them beyond the minimum needed to demonstrate the issue.

CVE credits and acknowledgements are granted at our discretion where a finding is original, reproducible and responsibly disclosed. A challenge score is not a certification or a job offer.

### 3. Fair play

- no attacking or doxxing other participants;
- no sharing accounts or automating submissions to game rankings;
- no using leaked credentials or third-party data you are not entitled to;
- no harassment, or content that is unlawful or hateful in challenge submissions.

We may disqualify entries, reset scores or ban accounts for breaches, and may suspend or end a challenge at any time.

### 4. No warranty and liability

Challenges are provided for education and fun, as is, without warranty of availability or fitness for any purpose. We are not liable for damage to your equipment, data loss or time spent, to the extent permitted by law.

You are responsible for complying with the law of your jurisdiction while participating.

## Terms of Service

Version 1.0 · effective 19 November 2026 · master terms · privacy policy

The rules that apply across everything we publish, plus a per-product terms page required for each product.

### 1. Who we are and what this document covers

These Terms of Service (“Terms”) govern the use of products, websites and services provided by Bartosz Osiej, trading as Hartwell Labs, an unregistered sole trader under Polish law (działalność nierejestrowana), based in Szczecin, Poland. Contact: contact@hartwell-labs.pl. A postal address for formal notices is available on request by e-mail.

They apply to everything we publish: open-source software, commercial add-ons, hosted services and content sites. Each product also has its own product terms, listed in section 2. Those product terms apply together with this document and prevail for that product if they conflict.

The current version is always available at hartwell-labs.pl/terms, free of charge, in a form you can download, store and print.

Definitions. “Product” means software, a hosted service or content we provide. “Account” means your access credentials. “Consumer” means a natural person acting outside their trade, business or profession. “Content” means data, files and materials you submit to a service.

### 2. Products and their terms

Every product has its own terms. The table is the authoritative index; if a product page links elsewhere, the link in this table wins.

| Product | Licence / model | Terms |
|---|---|---|

Open-source products are released under the MIT License. For those products the licence governs your rights in the code, and these Terms cover only the surrounding relationship: orders, payment, support expectations and liability. Commercial add-ons and hosted access are governed by the product terms and the agreement presented at purchase.

### 3. Accounts and eligibility

You must be at least 16 years old, or have the consent of a parent or guardian, to create an Account, and legally capable of entering a binding contract.

Provide accurate information and keep it current. You are responsible for keeping credentials confidential and for activity under your Account, unless the compromise was caused by our failure.

An Account belongs to one legal entity; transferring it requires our written consent. We may refuse or revoke access where required by law, sanctions or security.

### 4. Acceptable use

Use our products lawfully and as intended. You must not:

- infringe intellectual property, privacy or other rights of third parties;
- publish or distribute unlawful content, including child sexual abuse material, incitement to violence or hatred, or malware;
- send unsolicited bulk mail, phish, spoof senders, or commit fraud;
- access systems, accounts or data you are not authorised to access, or bypass limits and security controls;
- run network attacks, scans or penetration tests against us without prior written permission;
- resell or proxy access to a paid service unless its terms allow it;
- scrape at a rate that degrades a service, or in breach of robots directives or applicable licences;
- use a service to build a competing product by extracting non-public functionality or data.

Security tooling we publish is dual-use. Using it against systems you do not own or have written authorisation to test is your responsibility and may be a criminal offence.

You are responsible for your Content and for having a lawful basis to process it, including any consent required from individuals.

We may take proportionate protective action — rate limiting, blocking abuse or suspending an Account — and will tell you without undue delay unless a security or legal restriction prevents it.

### 5. Prices, taxes and payment

Prices are shown in EUR, USD or PLN and, where applicable, include VAT or other taxes. You are responsible for taxes your jurisdiction imposes that we do not collect.

Payments are processed by third-party providers, in particular Polar and Stripe. Where a provider acts as merchant of record, its terms also apply and we provide access to the buyer it authorises.

Subscriptions and paid add-ons renew automatically for the next billing period unless cancelled before it ends. Cancelling stops future charges; it does not refund the current period.

We may change prices for future periods with at least 14 days’ notice. Changes never apply retroactively to a period already paid for.

If a payment fails or is reversed, we may suspend paid access after notice and a reasonable opportunity to pay.

### 6. Your right to cancel (consumers)

If you are a consumer in the European Economic Area, the United Kingdom or another jurisdiction granting a cooling-off period, you may withdraw from a distance contract within 14 days without giving a reason. Write to contact@hartwell-labs.pl; no specific form is required.

For digital content and digital services supplied immediately, the withdrawal right ends only if you gave prior express consent to immediate supply, acknowledged that you lose the right, and we confirmed that acknowledgement. Those confirmations are collected at checkout. If they are not collected, your 14-day right remains intact.

We refund within 14 days of your notice, using the same payment method, unless you agree otherwise. We may withhold a refund until we have evidence that supply has stopped.

The right does not apply where the law excludes it, for example for a service fully performed at your express request before the period expired.

For free and open-source software there is nothing to refund; the MIT License governs that use.

### 7. Delivery, updates and support

Paid licences and access details are delivered electronically, normally within 24 hours of payment, to the e-mail address in your order or through the licence portal.

Support and update scope depends on the product and plan. Open-source projects receive community support with no guaranteed response time. Paid add-ons follow the response times stated at purchase.

Updates may change behaviour; material changes are described in release notes. We may retire a free product or service with at least 30 days’ notice on its page.

### 8. Intellectual property

Our products, documentation, designs and trademarks are protected by law. Except where a licence grants more, you receive a non-exclusive, non-transferable, revocable right to use a product as your plan allows.

Open-source components are licensed under their own terms, and nothing here reduces the rights those licences grant you. Proprietary modules are governed by LICENSE.commercial and the EULA shipped with the package.

Do not remove proprietary notices, reverse engineer beyond what law permits, or circumvent licence enforcement.

You keep ownership of your Content and grant us a limited licence to process it solely to operate the service for you. Feedback and bug reports may be used without restriction or payment, provided they contain no confidential information.

### 9. Data protection

Our Privacy Policy explains what personal data we process and why. We comply with the GDPR and applicable data protection law.

Where we process personal data on your behalf, we act as processor under a data processing agreement, available on request. Infrastructure subprocessors are listed in the Privacy Policy.

We apply measures appropriate to the risk, but no service is perfectly secure. Use unique credentials and multi-factor authentication where available, and keep your own backups of business-critical data.

### 10. Availability

We work to keep services available and schedule maintenance to minimise disruption, announcing planned downtime where practical.

Unless a plan states otherwise, hosted services run on a best-effort basis without a guaranteed service level. This does not reduce consumer rights relating to conformity.

We are not responsible for interruptions caused by force majeure, infrastructure provider failures, denial-of-service attacks, acts of authorities or your own configuration.

### 11. Suspension, termination and changes

We may suspend access immediately if you breach the law or these Terms, if a service or other users are at risk, if payment is overdue, or if an authority requires it. We will state the reason unless prohibited.

For breaches that are not obvious or urgent, we ask you to remedy them within 14 days and may terminate if you do not.

You may cancel at any time, effective at the end of the paid period. Refunds for unused periods follow the law and the applicable product terms.

After termination we make your Content available for export for 30 days where technically feasible, then delete it in line with the Privacy Policy and legal retention duties.

We may modify these Terms for legal, security or product reasons. Material changes are announced at least 14 days in advance by e-mail or in-product notice. You may cancel before they take effect; continued use afterwards means acceptance.

### 12. Liability

We are liable as required by law. To the extent permitted, our aggregate liability for claims relating to a paid product is limited to the fees you paid for it in the 12 months before the event, and for free products to EUR 100.

- Stopka: tło `--bg-subtle`, górna linia `--border`, siatka wielokolumnowa + cienka linia legalna.
- Przyciski: wysokość 44px, `border-radius: 10px`, `font-weight: 600`; `.btn-primary` wypełniony akcentem, `.btn-secondary` z obramowaniem.
- Breakpointy w CSS: `@media (max-width: 720px)`, `@media (max-width: 820px)`, `@media (max-width: 420px)` — na wąskich ekranach nawigacja w nagłówku jest ukrywana.

- Stopka: tło `--bg-subtle`, górna linia `--border`, siatka wielokolumnowa + cienka linia legalna.
- Przyciski: wysokość 44px, `border-radius: 10px`, `font-weight: 600`; `.btn-primary` wypełniony akcentem, `.btn-secondary` z obramowaniem.
- Breakpointy w CSS: `@media (max-width: 720px)`, `@media (max-width: 820px)`, `@media (max-width: 420px)` — na wąskich ekranach nawigacja w nagłówku jest ukrywana.

### 3. Page structure (in document order)

1. **Header** — sticky, logo (SVG sześciokąt + zygzak sygnału) po lewej, nawigacja pośrodku, przycisk GitHub po prawej.
   - Elementy: `Hartwell Labs` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/`, `Products` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/products`, `Firmware` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/firmware`, `Catalog` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/catalog`, `Docs` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/docs`, `Security` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/security`, `Company` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/company`, `GitHub ↗` → `https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs`
2. **Footer** — tło `--bg-subtle`, kolumny: (proste) (4 linków), na dobie fine-print z licencją i krajem.

### 4. Interactive elements

- 1 linków zewnętrznych (GitHub, PyPI, crates.io, sklepy) — otwierane w tej samej karcie.
- Brak formularzy, brak JS zależności poza `assets/site.js` i `challenge.js`.
- `challenge.js` jest skryptem łupieżczym — nie ładuj go przy renderowaniu.

- Na stronie jest JSON-LD (`application/ld+json`) z typem `Organization` / `WebSite` / `SoftwareApplication`.

# TrustNode — a Solana-like validator written from scratch in Rust | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Trusted compute · Rust*

# Built to understand, not to fork.

A Solana-style validator written from scratch in Rust: proof-of-history clock, Tower BFT consensus, Sealevel-style parallel execution, Turbine propagation with real Reed–Solomon erasure coding, CRDS gossip over UDP, a fee-priority mempool and an SBF-inspired program executor. Not a wrapper. Not a fork. Every line mine.

[Source on GitHub ↩](https://github.com/BartoszOsiej/TrustNode) → [Documentation](https://wiki.hartwell-labs.pl/projects/solana-validator)

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **12** | crates in the Cargo workspace |
| **228** | tests, all public |
| **~1M** | PoH hashes per second |
| **MIT** | licensed, fully public |

## Eleven subsystems, all real.

*What is inside*

Every cryptographic path is implemented, not stubbed: transactions are Ed25519-verified, votes are signed before they touch state, gossip messages that fail verification are counted and dropped without a reply.

#### Proof of History

A verifiable delay function: N sequential SHA-256 hashes per tick. Verification re-hashes N times and checks the result matches.

#### Tower BFT

Fork choice with lockouts — every vote on the same fork doubles the lockout, so switching forks gets expensive. Finality at two-thirds supermajority.

#### Sealevel-style scheduler

Conflict analysis over read/write account sets. Disjoint transactions batch together; write conflicts serialise. Slot-based with a compute budget.

#### Turbine + Reed–Solomon

Systematic RS over GF(256): any k of n shards reconstruct the block exactly, or the decoder returns None. Shreds are signed and verified on receipt.

#### CRDS gossip

Cluster Replicated Data Store with versioning, timeouts, push/pull and ping/pong — every outgoing message signed.

#### Accounts DB

Append-only store with a DashMap index for O(1) lookups and a Merkle tree over state for a verifiable state root.

#### Fee-priority mempool

Transaction fees are charged against the real accounts DB even when an instruction later fails — because that is Solana semantics.

#### Program executor

A unified native dispatcher with a System program (real SOL transfers, account creation) and an SPL-like Token program. No SBF runtime, so an unsupported program fails honestly instead of faking an Ok.

#### JSON-RPC 2.0

Account queries over a real server, backed by the same state the consensus path commits to.

## Tests first, then the node.

*Run it*

228 tests across the workspace, cargo clippy -D warnings, cargo audit with zero advisories, and CI on Linux and macOS with --locked, plus CodeQL and the OpenSSF Scorecard.

```console
cargo test --workspace
```

```console
cargo bench -- --bench
```

## Research-grade, on purpose.

*What it is not*

No SBF runtime, no QUIC (the transport is real UDP), no snapshot loading, and nothing tuned for production throughput. It has never run on mainnet and we do not claim it has — the README says plainly: do not use it for real transactions or staking. What it demonstrates is that the architecture can be held in one head, end to end.

---

| `--amber` | `#d97706` | ostrzeżenie |
| `--amber-soft` | `#fffbeb` | tło ostrzeżenia |

Motyw jest **jasny** (białe tło). Uwaga: `<meta name="theme-color">` na stronie deklaruje `#0a0e14` (ciemny) i jest niespójne z faktycznym, jasnym CSS-em — przy renderowaniu miej na uwadze, że jasny to stan poprawny.

### 2. Typography and layout

- Body: **Inter** (400/500/600/700), 16px, `line-height: 1.65`, kolor `--txt`.
- Kod inline i bloki: **JetBrains Mono** (400/600).
- Oba kroje z Google Fonts, z `preconnect` do `fonts.googleapis.com` i `fonts.gstatic.com`.
- `.container`: `max-width: 1100px`, wycentrowany, padding 24px po bokach.
- Nagłówek: sticky, wysokość **64px**, tło `rgba(255,255,255,.88)` z `backdrop-filter: blur(10px)`, dolna linia 1px `--border`, `z-index: 50`.
- Stopka: tło `--bg-subtle`, górna linia `--border`, siatka wielokolumnowa + cienka linia legalna.
- Przyciski: wysokość 44px, `border-radius: 10px`, `font-weight: 600`; `.btn-primary` wypełniony akcentem, `.btn-secondary` z obramowaniem.
- Breakpointy w CSS: `@media (max-width: 720px)`, `@media (max-width: 820px)`, `@media (max-width: 420px)` — na wąskich ekranach nawigacja w nagłówku jest ukrywana.

### 3. Page structure (in document order)

1. **Header** — sticky, logo (SVG sześciokąt + zygzak sygnału) po lewej, nawigacja pośrodku, przycisk GitHub po prawej.
   - Elementy: `Hartwell Labs` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/`, `Products` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/products`, `Firmware` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/firmware`, `Catalog` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/catalog`, `Docs` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/docs`, `Security` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/security`, `Company` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/company`, `GitHub ↩` → `https://github.com/BartoszOsiej/TrustNode`
2. **Hero** — blok `max-width: 760px`, padding `88px 0 72px`.
   - Eyebrow (kicker, `--txt-3`, wersaliki): _Trusted compute · Rust_
   - H1: _Built to understand, not to fork._ (krój 44–68px, `letter-spacing: -.02em`)
   - Lede (`--txt-2`, ~19px): _A Solana-style validator written from scratch in Rust: proof-of-history clock, Tower BFT consensus, Sealevel-style parallel execution, Turbine propagation with _
   - przycisk główny: **Source on GitHub ↩** → `https://github.com/BartoszOsiej/TrustNode`
   - przycisk drugorzędny: **Documentation** → `https://wiki.hartwell-labs.pl/projects/solana-validator`
3. **Pasek statystyk** — pełna szerokość, tło `--bg-subtle`, linie `--border` góra/dół, 4 kafelków. Każdy kafelek: duża liczba (`.n`, akcent/tekst) + podpis (`.l`, `--txt-3`).
   - **12** — crates in the Cargo workspace
   - **228** — tests, all public
   - **~1M** — PoH hashes per second
   - **MIT** — licensed, fully public
4. **Sekcja `#stack`** — *Eleven subsystems, all real.*
   - Kicker: _What is inside_ (11–12px, wersaliki, `--txt-3`)
   - Zawartość: 9 kart `.prod` (siatka, obramowanie 1px, `border-radius: 12px`, padding 20/22px, hover = zmiana koloru obramowania + cień)
5. **Sekcja `#start`** — *Tests first, then the node.*
   - Kicker: _Run it_ (11–12px, wersaliki, `--txt-3`)
   - Zawartość: 2 bloków `.cmd` (ciemny kod `#0f172a`, przycisk **COPY** kopiujący do schowka)
6. **Sekcja `#honest`** — *Research-grade, on purpose.*
   - Kicker: _What it is not_ (11–12px, wersaliki, `--txt-3`)
   - Zawartość: tekst (1 akapitów)
7. **Footer** — tło `--bg-subtle`, kolumny: Products, Resources, Company (9 linków), na dobie fine-print z licencją i krajem.

### 4. Interactive elements

- 2 przycisków **COPY** (`assets/site.js` → `navigator.clipboard.writeText`, tekst zmienia się na *COPIED* na 1400 ms). Każdy trzyma komendę w atrybucie `data-code`.
- 2 linków zewnętrznych (GitHub, PyPI, crates.io, sklepy) — otwierane w tej samej karcie.
- Brak formularzy, brak JS zależności poza `assets/site.js` i `challenge.js`.
- `challenge.js` jest skryptem łupieżczym — nie ładuj go przy renderowaniu.

### 5. Metadata for AI consumers

- `<title>`, `<meta name="description">`, `<link rel="canonical">` — patrz frontmatter.
- Na stronie jest JSON-LD (`application/ld+json`) z typem `Organization` / `WebSite` / `SoftwareApplication`.
- Strona jest dostępna również jako ten plik `.md` oraz w `/llms-full.txt`.
